subject: English
topic: Spotting Errors — Advanced Grammar (SSC CGL Tier 2 Set II, W11 B1)

questions.stem:
In each sentence, one part is underlined. Find the part with the grammatical error. If there is no error, choose D.

'The committee (A) have decided to (B) postpone its (C) annual meeting.' / (D) No error
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Committee' is a collective noun that takes a singular verb in standard Indian/SSC English. Correct: 'The committee HAS decided to postpone its annual meeting.' Note: In British English, collective nouns can take plural verbs, but SSC follows Indian/American convention where collective nouns are singular. The pronoun 'its' (C) is correct because 'committee' is treated as singular throughout the sentence — so 'its' is consistent and correct.

questions.stem:
Find the error:
'Neither the manager nor the employees (A) was present (B) at the meeting (C) yesterday.' / (D) No error

options.option_text: A — Neither the manager nor the employees

questions.explanation: B is correct. The rule for 'Neither...nor' and 'Either...or': the verb agrees with the subject CLOSEST to it (the nearer subject rule). Here, the subject closer to the verb is 'the employees' (plural). So the verb should be 'WERE present', not 'was'. Correct: 'Neither the manager nor the employees WERE present at the meeting yesterday.' Trap: Students apply singular verb because 'neither' sounds singular — but the nearer-subject rule overrides this.

questions.stem:
Find the error:
'He is one of those students (A) who performs (B) exceptionally well (C) in every examination.' / (D) No error
questions.explanation: B is correct. In the construction 'one of those + plural noun + relative clause', the relative pronoun 'who/that' refers to the PLURAL noun ('students'), not to 'one'. So the verb after 'who' must be plural: 'who PERFORM'. Correct: 'He is one of those students who perform exceptionally well...' Trap: Students make the verb singular because 'he is ONE' — but the antecedent of 'who' is 'those students', not 'he/one'.

questions.stem:
Find the error:
'Having finished (A) the assignment, (B) the television was switched on (C) by the students.' / (D) No error

options.option_text: B — the television was switched on

questions.explanation: B is correct. This is a dangling participle error. 'Having finished the assignment' is a participial phrase that must describe the subject of the main clause. But the subject of the main clause is 'the television' — and the television cannot finish an assignment. Correct: 'Having finished the assignment, THE STUDENTS switched on the television.' The subject (students) must follow immediately after the participial phrase.

questions.stem:
Find the error:
'The number of candidates (A) who have applied (B) for the post are (C) surprisingly large.' / (D) No error
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'The number of...' takes a singular verb. (Compare: 'A number of candidates HAVE applied' where 'a number' = many → plural). 'The number' is always singular. Correct: 'The number of candidates who have applied for the post IS surprisingly large.' Trap: Students see 'candidates (plural)' and use 'are' — but the subject is 'the number' (singular), not 'candidates'.

questions.stem:
Find the error:
'She is senior than me (A) by three years (B) and works in (C) the same department.' / (D) No error

options.option_text: A — She is senior than me

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Senior', 'junior', 'superior', 'inferior', 'prior', 'anterior', 'posterior' are Latin comparatives — they NEVER take 'than'. They take 'TO'. Correct: 'She is senior TO me by three years.' Similarly: 'He is junior to me'; 'This product is inferior to that one'. The use of 'than' with Latin comparatives is a classic SSC grammar trap.

questions.stem:
Find the error:
'Each of the students (A) in the class (B) have submitted (C) their assignments on time.' / (D) No error
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Each' is always singular and takes a singular verb. 'Each of the students HAS submitted HIS/HER assignment on time.' Both 'have' (plural verb) and 'their' (plural pronoun) are wrong. Correct: 'Each of the students in the class HAS submitted HIS/HER assignment on time.' Trap: The plural noun 'students' draws students toward 'have' and 'their', but the subject is 'each' (singular).

questions.stem:
Find the error:
'No sooner did the teacher enter (A) than the students (B) stood up (C) respectfully.' / (D) No error

options.option_text: A — No sooner did the teacher enter

questions.explanation: D is correct. 'No sooner...than' is the correct paired conjunction — 'no sooner' always pairs with 'than', not 'when'. The inversion after 'no sooner' ('did the teacher enter' rather than 'the teacher entered') is also correct — negative adverbials at the start of a clause require subject-auxiliary inversion. This sentence is fully grammatically correct. Trap: Some expect 'when' instead of 'than'; others question the inversion — both are correct features of formal English.

questions.stem:
Find the error:
'If I was you, (A) I would not have (B) accepted (C) that offer.' / (D) No error
questions.explanation: A is correct. In a subjunctive/conditional (hypothetical/unreal) clause with the verb 'to be', 'were' must be used for ALL persons, not 'was'. Correct: 'If I WERE you, I would not have accepted that offer.' The subjunctive mood ('were') signals a hypothetical/contrary-to-fact condition. 'If I was you' = incorrect (uses indicative 'was' where subjunctive 'were' is required). Trap: Many speakers say 'if I was' in informal speech, but SSC tests formal/written grammar.

questions.stem:
Find the error:
'The police (A) has arrested (B) three suspects (C) in connection with the robbery.' / (D) No error
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Police' is a plural noun (it refers to a body of officers, always treated as plural). Correct: 'The police HAVE arrested three suspects...' Similarly: 'The cattle are grazing'; 'The people were angry'; 'The clergy have voted'. These are plural-only nouns with no singular form. Trap: 'The police' sounds like a single entity and students use 'has' — but grammar rules classify 'police' as plural in form and concord.
